canonical_statement: The study compared a body-weight-adjusted intravenous heparin nomogram with a standard-care nomogram for achieving prompt therapeutic anticoagulation in acute coronary syndromes.
Eligible participants were hospitalized patients intended to receive intravenous heparin for coronary artery syndromes; the randomized cohort did not receive thrombolytic therapy.

population.label: Hospitalized patients intended to receive IV heparin for coronary artery syndromes
inclusion_criteria: Intended treatment with intravenous heparin for a coronary artery syndrome
exclusion_criteria: Receipt of thrombolytic therapy in the randomized study cohort

canonical_statement: This was a prospective randomized comparison conducted at University of Missouri Hospital and Clinics among patients enrolled from July 1994 through February 1995.
The study included 64 patients; 31 were male and the reported mean age was 60 years with a dispersion value of 11.4 years.

population.label: Randomized acute coronary syndrome cohort

canonical_statement: Heparin indications were unstable angina (30 patients), rule-out myocardial infarction (18), acute myocardial infarction without thrombolytic therapy (4), and miscellaneous indications such as post-angioplasty or atherectomy (12).

population.label: Randomized acute coronary syndrome cohort

canonical_statement: APTT was measured at baseline and at 6, 12, 18, 24, and 48 hours, with heparin dosing adjusted by the assigned nomogram.
The study therapeutic goal was an APTT of 60-90 seconds.
The laboratory reported a normal APTT range of 23.7-33.4 seconds.

APTT specimens were collected in buffered-citrate tubes and measured with an automated Organon-Teknika reagent on an MLA 900 C coagulation system; the authors reported a correlation coefficient of 0.999 between mean APTT values from the two automated systems using the 1992 College of American Pathologists database.
Plasma heparin concentrations were measured with a chromogenic heparin assay using study heparin to establish standard curves, and determinations were performed in duplicate.
Randomization was implemented by drawing an envelope containing either the standard-care or weight-adjusted nomogram from a large set of envelopes after consent.
Staff nurses knew the assigned nomogram, weighed patients, calculated doses, and adjusted infusion rates using preprinted orders.
After study completion, researchers blinded to nomogram assignment reviewed medical records for hospital complications.
The study defined thrombocytopenia as a decrease in platelet count below 100,000 U/L, using the unit notation printed in the source.

outcome.definition: Decrease in platelet count <100,000 U/L as printed in the source

canonical_statement: Major hemorrhage was defined by transfusion requirement, a hemoglobin decrease greater than 2 g/L as printed in the source, or clinical hemorrhage in the retroperitoneum, cranium, or prosthetic joint.

outcome.definition: Transfusion, hemoglobin decrease >2 g/L as printed, or clinical hemorrhage in specified critical sites

canonical_statement: Minor hemorrhage was defined as reported bleeding that did not meet the major-hemorrhage criteria.

outcome.definition: Reported bleeding not meeting major hemorrhage criteria

canonical_statement: Continuous variables were compared with the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, discrete variables with Fisher exact testing, and p<0.05 was considered significant; the authors cited the laboratory APTT ceiling of 150 seconds as a reason for rank-based analysis.
The authors reported no significant baseline differences between randomized groups in age, weight, sex, heparin indication, or baseline APTT.

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that a weight-adjusted heparin nomogram produced more effective early anticoagulation than the standard-care nomogram in patients with acute coronary artery syndromes.

Because of high early APTT values, the authors reported revising their weight-adjusted nomogram by reducing the initial bolus from 80 to 70 units/kg; this revision was not evaluated in the randomized comparison.

The authors reported revising the post-study protocol so that an APTT below 1.2 times control would trigger an infusion-rate increase of 6 units/kg/hour rather than 4 units/kg/hour; this change was not tested in the trial.

The authors reported revising the post-study protocol so that an APTT in the range they printed as 1.2-2.3 times control would trigger an infusion-rate increase of 4 units/kg/hour rather than 2 units/kg/hour; this change was not tested in the trial.

The authors also reported a post-study change for APTT 1.5-2 times control: increase the infusion by 2 units/kg/hour and give a 20-units/kg bolus rather than giving the bolus alone; this change was not tested in the randomized trial.

The authors stated that the ideal heparin nomogram had not yet been developed but argued that weight-based dosing offered the best prospect for early effective anticoagulation in acute coronary artery syndromes.
